lesson.title: Combining Dictionaries the Modern Way
lesson.summary: Beyond update(), Python 3.9 and later offers the | and |= operators to merge dictionaries, with | producing a brand new dictionary instead of changing one in place.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter showed that update() merges one dictionary into another by changing the first dictionary in place and returning None. That is exactly what you want when you already have a dictionary you intend to keep modifying. But sometimes you want a merge that produces a fresh dictionary while leaving both original dictionaries untouched, for example when you are combining a set of defaults with a set of user overrides and want to keep the original defaults around unchanged for next time. Since Python 3.9, the | operator does exactly that.

defaults = {"volume": 50, "brightness": 70}
user_settings = {"brightness": 90, "contrast": 60}

merged = defaults | user_settings
print(merged)
print(defaults)

This prints {'volume': 50, 'brightness': 90, 'contrast': 60}, then {'volume': 50, 'brightness': 70}. The merge keeps "volume" from defaults since user_settings never mentions it, takes 90 for "brightness" from user_settings since the right-hand dictionary wins any collision, and adds "contrast" from user_settings since defaults never had it. Crucially, the second print shows defaults still holds its original brightness of 70: the | operator built merged as an entirely new dictionary and never touched defaults at all, which is the key difference from update().

When you do want to update a dictionary in place but prefer the operator syntax over calling .update(), Python provides |= as a shorthand.

defaults |= user_settings
print(defaults)

This prints {'volume': 50, 'brightness': 90, 'contrast': 60}. Now defaults itself has been changed, exactly as if we had written defaults.update(user_settings). In both the | and |= forms, the same rule from update() still applies to overlapping keys: whichever dictionary is on the right supplies the final value.

As a summary rule: reach for .update() or |= when you intend to change an existing dictionary in place, and reach for plain | when you want a new merged dictionary while leaving the originals exactly as they were. Also remember that | and |= for dictionaries require Python 3.9 or later; in older code you will still see update() used for every kind of merge.
